## Introduction {.unnumbered}

In this problem set, you will apply machine learning (ML) methods to the problem
of predicting school-wide test scores on NYS standardized mathematics exams, 
given geographic and socioeconomic information about the student population. 

Along the way, we will review some basic ML terminology, take a closer look
at how qualitative features like school district can be transformed for use in
quantiative contexts, compare a variety of linear regression methods under 
different loss functions, benchmark against a basic non-linear model, and 
estimate the out-of-sample performance of different models for the same data.

## Data Files {.unnumbered}

For this problem set, you will make use of the NYSED Math Scores data posted
[here](./data/ps01_nysed.csv). This data set is extracted from standardized
math test scores from (essentially) all public schools in New York 
State.[^complete] For each school, I have reported the percent of students who 
achieve passing ('proficient') status for that exam, as well as a variety of 
other pieces of aggregate demographic data about the student body of that 
school. The full data set looks like this: 

[^complete]: I have restricted the data set to only those schools that choose
to report the full set of demographic variables in the data set, so there are no
missing values to deal with. 

```{r}
#| echo: false
NYSED <- read_csv("problem_sets/data/ps01_nysed.csv")
glimpse(NYSED)
```

Our goal will be to use all of these variables to predict the pass rate
`PERCENT_PROFICIENT`. Note that some of the variables are _quantitative_
while others are _qualitative_, *e.g.*, the school name and district name. Finally, 
note that I have rescaled percentages so that quantities like `PERCENT_PROFICIENT`
or `PERCENT_ENGLISH_LANGUAGE_LEARNERS` are shown as "75", "13", "50", "0" instead
of "0.75", "0.13", "0.5", "0". 

You can read this data set directly off this website. In `R`, simply run: 

```{r}

```

## **$K$-Nearest Neighbor Methods** (5 points)

In class, we introduced most of our ML concepts through one foundational method
(OLS). In this assignment, we are going to compare OLS with a very different,
but no less foundational, method called $K$-Nearest Neighbors (K-NN). 

K-NN formalizes a simple idea: to make a prediction, remember what happened at
the most similar point in the past. Specifically, when given a new point 
$\tilde{\bx}$, we can search our training data for the 'most similar' 
point $\bx_{\text{NN}}$ and use its label as our prediction for $\tilde{\bx}$: 
$\hat{y} = y_{\text{NN}}$. This is _one_ nearest-neighbor prediction (1-NN) 
because we found the _one_ most similar point from our training data. In practice,
we usually find several similar points (3, 5, or 7) and take their _average_ to
make our predictions. This is a bit less messy (random) than using a single point, 
while still being nearly as flexible as 1-NN. 

The $K$-NN family of methods is opposite to OLS in many ways: 

- While OLS reduces the (potentially) large training data down to a few 
  coefficients, $K$-NN has no coefficients
- Making predictions with OLS is easy (just a few multiplications and additions)
  while making predictions with $K$-NN can be slow if we have to review the
  entire training set every time we want to use it
- When fit to non-linear relationships, OLS necessarily loses some information
  (by forcing things into a single plane) while $K$-NN can fit any shape with
  enough data.[^universal]
  

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 2"}

**Fit $K$-NN to the NYSED Prediction Task**

- Fit $1$-NN to the NYSED Prediction Task (using only the numeric features).
  What is the training error? Why?
- Fit `r NROW(NYSED)`-NN to the NYSED Prediction Task (again using only numeric
  features) and look at the predictions on the training data? What do you see?
  Why?
- When faced with many features, $K$-NN can be slow to implement so many 
  approximate algorithms have been developed. 
  
  Find an _approximate_ $K$-NN algorithm and compare it to 'actual' $K$-NN for
  several values of $K$ (1, 3, 5, and 7 are reasonable choices). Make sure to
  compare predictions, training error, and the time it takes to make predictions.
  

For this problem, you may use pre-written $K$-NN methods. You do not need to
implement $K$-NN from scratch. 

:::
  
[^universal]: For this reason, we say $K$-NN is _universally consistent_. As we
will discuss, this is a double-edged sword: it can fit _any_ pattern, but it can
also fit _any_ noise. 

## **Encodings and Tabular Representations** (5 points)

The majority of methods discussed in this course require *tabular* data output. 
That is, data arranged in a two-dimensional grid where one axis (typically row) 
indexes observations and the other (typically column) indexes different
features of the data. In each cell of the resulting table, a single (scalar)
value reflects the value of a specific feature for a specific observation. 
*E.g.*, 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

set.seed(3106)
iris_sub <- iris |> 
    mutate(Species = str_to_title(Species)) |> 
    group_by(Species) |> 
    slice_sample(n=4) |>
    ungroup()

iris_sub |> 
    gt(id="tbl_iris1") |>
    cols_label(Sepal.Length = "Sepal Length (mm)", 
               Sepal.Width = "Sepal Width (mm)", 
               Petal.Length = "Petal Length (mm)", 
               Petal.Width="Petal Width (mm)") |> 
    tab_header(md("**Iris Flower Morphometrics**")) |> 
    tab_source_note(md("Fisher, R.A. (1936) 'The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems', *Annals of Human Genetics* 7(2), pp.179-188. 1936. DOI:[10.1111/j.1469-1809.1936.tb02137.x](https://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-1809.1936.tb02137.x)")) |>
    tab_footnote("(Species-stratified sample of 12 rows)")
```

While this format is sufficient for most data manipulation tasks, a little
more pre-processing is required before fitting mathematical models. 
Specifically, *qualitative* features need to be transformed into *quantitative*
values through a process called _encoding_. 

The most common type of encoding is "one-hot encoding" in which a column
is created for _each_ possible value of _each_ qualitative feature. *E.g.*,
in the table above, we might process the data into a format like: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(recipes)

recipe(~ ., data=iris_sub) |> 
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot=TRUE) |>
    prep() |> 
    bake(new_data=NULL) |>
    gt(id="iris_tbl2") |>
    cols_label(Sepal.Length = "Sepal Length (mm)", 
               Sepal.Width = "Sepal Width (mm)", 
               Petal.Length = "Petal Length (mm)", 
               Petal.Width="Petal Width (mm)")
```

One-hot encoding is useful, but it can quickly make problems _explode_ in size.
(If you have 20 categorical features, each of which takes on 15 different values,
you now have 300 numerical features! Since many ML methods are quadratic in
run-time, this means your algorithm just became about 225 times slower!) 
This may not be the end of the world-computers are quite fast after all-but it
suggests that there may be a role for other approaches that avoid creating quite
so many features. 

One popular choice is _target_ encoding, in which the categorical variable 
is replaced by the average value of the response for that 'subgroup' of the data.
For instance, if we were trying to predict the Petal Length of the `iris` data
above, _target_ encoding would give us this data set instead: 

```{r}
iris_sub |> 
    group_by(Species) |> 
    mutate(Species = mean(Petal.Length)) |> 
    ungroup() |>
    gt(id="iris_tbl3") |>
    cols_label(Sepal.Length = "Sepal Length (mm)", 
               Sepal.Width = "Sepal Width (mm)", 
               Petal.Length = "Petal Length (mm)", 
               Petal.Width="Petal Width (mm)", 
               Species="Species (Target Encoded on Petal Length)")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 3"}

- Fit OLS to the NYSED Data using One-Hot Encoding for all qualitative features.

:::

## Estimating Out of Sample Performance with Cross-Validation (20 points)

Recall that our primary focus in this course is on developing models that perform
well _out-of-sample_, *i.e.*, on new 'test' data. Unfortunately, we do not 
always have an unlimited supply of 'new' data we can use for model evaluation
and instead have to find a way to use our existing data for both model fitting
and model evaluation. Doing this correctly can be a bit tricky: we want to avoid
testing the model on data it has already seen so we don't give it credit for
'teaching to the test.' 

But the fix is not too hard! We can split our data into two parts and use one 
for model fitting and the other for model evaluation in lieu of 'true' test 
data. The 'golden rule' here is simple: what is used to fit a model _cannot_ be
used to evaluate it and _vice versa_. In general, fitting a model is harder than
simply estimating its out-of-sample accuracy, so we don't use a straight
50/50 split, but it's hard to give a universal guideline.[^as_much] This is
known as the **hold-out** method. 

[^as_much]: In general, you want to use as much data as needed to get a good 
estimate of model performance, but no more; without having some *a priori* 
knowledge of the inherent difficulty (variance) of a problem, this is a bit
easier said than done. 

One criticism of the **hold-out** method is that it can be a bit wasteful and
a bit random. If we set 40% of our data aside for the holdout set, we are fitting
our model on only 60% as much data as we would hope to and this can make our 
predictions _much_ worse.[^pct] With 'large enough' data, this may not be a
problem, but 'large enough' is always relative to the model being fit and we 
would rather use a large data set to fit a flexible and powerful model; in 
other problems, data is scarce and spending 25-40% on model testing can 
significantly impair our ability to fit models at all. 

The method of [*cross-validation*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-validation_(statistics) (CV)
attempts to address some of these limitations. Rather than performing a single 
split, we first: 

- Split the entire data set into $K$ chunks of (roughly) equal size; 
- For $k = 1, \dots, K$:
  - Set one chunk aside for model evaluation
  - Use the other $K-1$ chunks to fit the model
  - Evaluate the model on the 'set aside' chunk and record the prediction error
- Average the prediction errors to get the *cross-validation* estimate of 
  prediction error. (It is also a good idea to put an error bar on this average.)
  
Visually, 

![From the `sklearn` Documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.5/_images/grid_search_cross_validation.png)

Note that because the model being evaluated is a bit different each of the $K$
times, it's best to think of cross-validation as estimating the accuracy of
a class of models rather than a single model. ('How well does _linear regression_
do on this problem?' rather than 'How well will this specific line do?')

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 4"}

**Implement 10-Fold Cross Validation to Estimate Prediction Performance on the NYSED Math Proficiency Task**

- Read [Chapter 4 of MLB](https://www.mlbenchmarks.org/04-holdout-method.html)
  for additional background on the holdout method
- Implement 10-fold cross validation to estimate the prediction error of OLS
  and 5-NN on the full NYSED data set 
  (all 9721 rows) using only the `NUMBER_*` features. How does the CV error 
  compare to the in-sample error? 
- Repeat your analysis using _all_ numeric features. How does the CV error 
  compare to the in-sample error? Does this make sense? Why or why not? 
- Repeat your analysis using _all_ features, except `SCHOOL_NAME` and 
  `DISTRICT_NAME`, using **one-hot** encoding. How does the
  CV error compare to the in-sample error? Does this make sense? Why or why not? 
- Repeat your analysis using _all_ features, except `SCHOOL_NAME` and 
  `DISTRICT_NAME`, using **target** encoding. (**NB** Do the encoding _within_ 
  each cross-validation fold, not _before_ splitting the data.) How does the
  CV error compare to the in-sample error? Does this make sense? Why or why not? 
- Text Answer: Why is it important to do target encoding _within_ each CV fold? 
  What would happen if we did target encoding before implementing CV? What would
  happen to our CV error and what would happen to our eventual test error?
  
For this whole assignment, you must implement CV 'by hand' and cannot use a 
built-in cross-validation function like `sklearn`'s `sklearn.model_selection.cross_validation`. 
  
:::
  
*Important*: When fitting CV for all features, make sure to avoid any 
"data leakage" during the encoding steps. You may need to look into concepts 
like _stratified sampling_. If a feature has too many values you can drop it
from your analysis, but just be sure to note that you did. 

[^pct]: Think of estimating the mean of a distribution. With 100 samples, the
standard error in our estimation of the mean is $\hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{100}$ from
the full data, but only $\hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{60}$ from the 'fitting' portion
of the data. This could increase our error by a factor of around 
$1.3 \approx \sqrt{100}/\sqrt{60}$ - that's the difference between success and
failure in many problems!

## Using Cross-Validation for Model Selection (15 points)

Another use of cross-validation is selecting certain 'hyperparameters'. 
_Hyperparameters_ in this context refers to decisions that are made before
the model encounters data: *e.g.*, we might pre-select which features to
include in a linear model before we actually use our data to estimate the
regression coefficients.[^fuzzy] Recalling our 'north star' of optimizing
predictions, we can try a reasonable range of values for a hyperparameter and
pick the one that gives the most accurate cross-validation predictions. 

There is, however, a slight risk here as the CV error we get is not an unbiased
estimate of the true prediction error. Remember: if we pick the values of the
model parameters to minimize our loss, we expect our future loss to be a bit 
worse; the same logic applies to selecting _hyperparameters_. To avoid this, we
should use a combination of CV + holdout. 

[^fuzzy]: If you think that this line can be a bit fuzzy in practice, you are
not wrong. Still, the idea of 'structural' vs 'ERM-driven' choices is an 
important one. 


::: {.callout-tip title="Question 5"}

- Now, compute the performance of $K_{\text{best}}$-NN on the 10% hold out data.

:::

You may use the fast (approximate) $K$-nearest neighbors from the previous
question. 



## Estimating LOCO Feature Importance (15 points)

In certain applications, it may be important to _interpret_ or _explain_
the output of an ML model. Because different models work differently and different
users require different types of interpretations, this is a challenging task for
which a variety of methods have been proposed.[^ga_iml] In this sub-problem, you
will explore a basic strategy sometimes called **LOCO** (Leave-One-Covariate-Out)
feature importance. 

The idea of LOCO is simple: a model is fit with and without a given feature and
compare its performance. If the performance of the model falls when a feature
is omitted, it is important; if the performance doesn't significantly change,
the feature is probably not too important to the model (or can be 'replaced' by
other features in the data). Since, as always, we are interested in 
out-of-sample performance, the LOCO score is typically computed within a 
cross-validation scheme, rather than simply comparing in-sample error. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Question 6"}

**Use LOCO to Determine the Relative Feature Importance of 5 Features in this Data Set**

- Select 5 features that you intuitively think would be the most important for
  this data set and state your _a priori_ ranking as to which will be the most
  important. (You can do more, but LOCO can become quite slow rather quickly
  so 5 is enough.)
- Using LOCO with a five-fold cross-validation step, compute the importance of
  each feature and create a figure to visualize your results. Your figure must
  include 'error bars' to capture the randomness in your CV error estimates. 
- Compare your LOCO results with your initial guess about feature importance. 
  Are they consistent? If no, why not? 
- Finally, compare your OLS-LOCO scores to KNN-LOCO on the same data. (You can
  fix $K$ to the value you determined previously and do not need to re-estimate 
  it.) Do your results change? Does this make sense?
  
:::

Statistics and Its Application* **11**, p.97-121 (2024).
